notes: Whole-WCS eta_WCS 92.7% and primary-to-secondary DC–DC subchain eta_DC-DC 95.5% are explicitly different boundaries in the same paper. Exact WCS planes are missing, so do not invent the stage coverage; the quantity and boundary-class mismatch are already decisive.

The approximately 63.3% vehicle-level traction energy replenishment share is a service ratio, not a conversion efficiency. It must not be ranked against the 12.4% laser-to-electric end-to-end efficiency.
The >20% passive AC-to-AC relay-to-receiver result excludes source conversion and receiver rectification; the approximately 5% DC-to-DC point includes the overall DC input to rectified DC output.

The 95.96% laser-driver stage efficiency is not a valid substitute for 12.4% end-to-end laser-to-electric performance over the 20 m optical path. The complete LPT meter planes/stage set are not fully identified in the abstract.

Qualification probe, not a cross-prototype ranking: this whole-WCS observation lacks exact input/output meter planes, a complete stage map, statistic and uncertainty. It is not eligible for strict leaderboard use until those omissions are resolved, even when the evaluator is asked to compare the record to itself.

The 50 kW Riekerk and 65 kW Zavrel devices are different rated power classes, in addition to incomplete meter planes, stage sets, matched load points, statistic and uncertainty. Their DC-to-DC labels do not justify ranking the 97%-range against the 95.5% point without a shared load condition and matched boundaries.

Qualification probe: the abstract's 13.86 μT scalar lacks probe position, orientation, reference frame, spatial region, averaging method, measured-vs-modelled method, frequency and uncertainty. Do not qualify it as a comparable exposure record or compliance finding.

Two mode-indexed maximum DC-to-DC efficiency values from one six-mode prototype. The abstract does not map mode indices to the three SAE power classes or state exact load powers, frequencies, gaps, meter planes or uncertainty. Do not infer that the 94.48% mode is inherently superior across power classes.

The 4.60 kW five-mode downscaled interoperability prototype and the 50 kW bus charger are different rated power classes and conditions. Mode-specific values, meter planes, test gaps and uncertainties are incomplete; the >80% threshold is not a point estimate for ranking against the 50 kW DC-DC range.
The 96.5% figure belongs to the wireless WPT mode; the 89.1% figure belongs to the separate wired LVDC converter mode. Reusing hardware does not make the conversion paths or test services the same.

The two-channel series array's 95.7% maximum at 4 kW aggregate output is not a fair direct comparison to Zavrel's 92.7% whole-WCS result at 65 kW. Their declared power points differ, and neither source abstract/table provides a fully matched meter-plane, statistic and uncertainty record.

The two-channel series array's approximately 95.7% maximum at 4 kW aggregate output is not a fair direct comparison to Zavrel's 92.7% whole-WCS value at 65 kW. The power points are different; exact input/output meter planes, statistic and uncertainty are also incomplete.

The 6 and 11 kW BIPT-link DC-DC bands differ in rated power class, battery voltage class, ground clearance and coil-to-coil air gap. A higher range endpoint at 11 kW is not evidence that the 11 kW class is superior; these are separate operating envelopes and lack a common exact meter plane, test point, statistic and uncertainty.

The Zhang 30 kW / 20 kHz bidirectional BIPT-link DC-DC band and Li 20 kW magnetic-integration prototype are different rated power classes and system topologies. Exact meter planes, load point, air gap, direction, stage set and test window are not matched. The 93.6-94.5% band is not evidence of superiority over the 90.58% Li result.

The paper compares SS and LCC simulation outputs on the same constant 90 km/h, 510 km case. It reports 0.14 and 0.15 kWh/km respectively, but the accessible model output does not define an exact meter plane/stage set, operating waveform and alignment details or uncertainty. Both values are simulations and cannot be promoted to measured road performance. This frozen case should remain UNRESOLVED rather than turn a simulated difference into a field/SOTA win.

The 31.3% MFB and 20.0% differential-regulation-coil temperature reductions are relative improvements against different paper-specific reference configurations. They must not be ranked by magnitude. Absolute temperatures, matched thermal load/soak, geometry, measurement planes, statistics and uncertainty are not aligned. Operating frequency, air gap, duration and other numeric conditions remain unreported, so this is also incomplete on operating conditions.

The 8.1% MFB and 18.2% differential-regulation-coil leakage-flux reductions use different paper-specific baselines and potentially different probe locations, spatial regions, averaging and conditions. The percentages are not a head-to-head ranking; matched field metrology and the underlying measurement definitions are required. Operating frequency, air gap, duration and other numeric conditions remain unreported, so this is also incomplete on operating conditions.

The HCMPC paper reports >90% efficiency across a 30-80 Ω load range, while the 430 W MLP/PSO paper reports a 93.5% maximum. Neither is a matched efficiency point: HCMPC power/frequency are unknown, Xu is a distinct 430 W/85 kHz prototype, exact meter planes and statistic are unresolved, and uncertainty is unreported. Do not rank the headline values.

HCMPC's <0.5% output-voltage error over a 30-80 Ω load range and the 50 W paper's <1% CC/CV steady-state error are different control quantities and test envelopes. They should not be ranked as one generic controller-error score without matched control objectives, output definitions, transient windows and reference load profiles.

The left observation is an author-derived relative magnetic-coupling operating-range reduction (>=34%) for a WPT3 VA / flush-mounted GA geometry comparison. The right observation is a measured DC-DC link efficiency range (94.0-95.7%) for a 6 kW WPT3-class VA. The two quantities are different; a coupling-range reduction is not an efficiency loss. Their power class, frequency, geometry and test conditions are also not matched.

One is average whole-system efficiency at 1 kW for a rectangular Tx; the other is peak DC-DC efficiency at 2 kW for a bipolar dynamic composite coupler. Power class, statistic, transmitter/receiver topology, exact meter planes and test profile differ. Do not rank 90.44% against 89.8%.

Along-track output-power fluctuation (2.73%) and output-voltage fluctuation (~3%) are different physical observables, test coordinate grids and dynamic prototype classes. The similar percentages do not establish equal power quality, output stability or service continuity.
